newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ DEFU undermined by coalition talks - economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ DEFU undermined by coalition talks - economists.

text.p: Economists say the forecasts in Monday's December Economic and Fiscal Update (DEFU) by Treasury could be out of date within days of release and the document is based on unrealistic assumptions, NZPA reported on Thursday.
NZPA said many economists have not bothered to prepare forecasts for the DEFU, which is usually a major event on the financial calendar.
Those who have, have revised down the operating surpluses expected in the 1996/97 year to between NZ$2.4 and $2.6 billion from the $2.87 billion forecast in the pre-election update (PREFU).
This is because Finance Minister Bill Birch signalled last week that the surpluses would be slightly lower and because the economy is perceived to have slowed.
The DEFU forecasts assume no change in government policy and economists said that while the assumption was understandable, it was also unrealistic once the new government is formed.

"Consensus seems to be that policy will change to varying degrees when a new government is formed. And as a result this (the DEFU) is really just a meter reading exercise," said David Drage, treasury economist at ANZ Bank.
He said the statement would provide a basis for the fiscal debate because it would provide an updated base line.
The update is expected to be about 100 pages in size, much smaller than it has been in previous years and it has been brought forward to earlier in the month than last year.
Nevertheless, it has the benefit of a full forecasting round. Treasury's post election update is not expected to be released until a new government is formed.

Bankers Trust said a $2.5 billion forecast surplus in the 1996/97 year would be a minor change and agrees that it is a "fairly safe bet that the next government will change fiscal policy, which means that the forecasts in the DEFU could be out of date within days of being published (if not before)".
The government's budget position has tracked close to forecast so far this year, despite a slowdown in the economy which traditionally reduces revenues and increases expenditure.
The fiscal outturn for the four months to November due on Friday is expected to show a surplus of $800 million.
The DEFU is also expected to include slight downward revisions to growth forecasts.

Bankers Trust expect Treasury to forecast growth of 2.5 percent between March 1996 and March 1997, on a quarter-on-quarter basis, down from the 3.2 percent previously and compared with the 2 percent predicted by the Reserve Bank on that basis.
Treasury's growth forecasts were regarded by some in the market as high and soft labour market and retail sales data is expected to have reinforced the case for a downgrade.
Birch said in last week's speech that growth was still expected to be well above two percent at the bottom of the business cycle.
Tony Alexander, chief economist at the Bank of New Zealand, said he had not bothered to prepare forecasts and he expected the DEFU to be a non-event.
"We're really waiting for the coalition talks outcome and the Reserve Bank December 17 statement. Overall, I don't think it's going to be significant".
Infometrics is forecasting a $1.5 billion surplus in 1997/98 if there is a Labour party-led coalition and a $2.4 billion surplus if there is a National party-led coalition.
